thesis: Qatar supplies roughly a fifth of seaborne LNG and its exports have collapsed ~96% since the Strait of Hormuz was effectively closed — 18 cargoes shipped versus 509 in the same period last year. QatarEnergy has extended force majeure into November and the damaged liquefaction trains are estimated to need three to five years of repair, about $20bn of annual revenue, with analysts now pushing the global gas rebalance from mid-2026 out to 2028. The only supply that can fill a multi-year hole of that size is US export capacity, which pulls domestic molecules to the coast and tightens Henry Hub. EQT is the largest US natural gas producer and the most direct liquid equity on that pull. The tape is already voting: on 2026-09-01, with SPY -0.69% and QQQ -1.27%, EQT closed +2.60% and Antero +3.46%. EQT sits 18.5% below its 180-day high of 68.24 while Cheniere, the already-consensus LNG expression, is within 2.2% of its own high — the producers have not re-rated and the midstream has.
key_risk: This is a war trade wearing a structural costume. A ceasefire that reopens Hormuz would not repair Qatar’s trains, but it would collapse the *fear* premium in gas well before the physical shortage resolves, and EQT would give back the move in days. Henry Hub is also a domestic price: US export capacity is physically capped in the near term, so the pull-through is real but slower and smaller than the European TTF move implies.
counter_argument: The strongest case against: US gas is not one market with global LNG, it is a separate basin joined by a bottleneck, and that bottleneck is liquefaction capacity that is already running flat out. If no new US trains come online this winter, higher TTF prices simply widen the netback for Cheniere and the terminal owners rather than lifting the wellhead price EQT receives — which is precisely why LNG the ticker is at its highs and EQT is not. The counter to the counter is that the shortage now has a multi-year runway, which is long enough for contracting and capacity decisions to reach the producer.

thesis: Rate-sensitive equities have not repriced for the rate move that has already happened. IYR closed below both its 20-day (104.17) and 50-day (104.41) on 2026-09-01 with the two averages converging overhead, which turns them into a single well-defined resistance shelf to short into. REITs also carry real floating-rate and near-term refinancing exposure, so a hike is a cash-flow event for them and not merely a discount-rate one.

If Iran and the US reach a ceasefire, crude gives back the spike, the inflation impulse and the hike odds unwind together, and IYR gaps up through 106.40 before the US open with no chance to exit at the stop. The low 1.02% ATR also means the 2.4-ATR stop is only 3.9% away in percentage terms — this instrument does not give much room.
counter_argument: The strongest case against: an oil shock is a growth shock, and if the Fed hikes into it the curve should bull-flatten with the long end rallying — which would make REITs, priced off the 10y rather than the funds rate, the wrong short. Real estate is also a real asset, and a genuine inflation regime eventually lifts rents and replacement cost. Both are true over a year; neither is likely to assert itself inside the two weeks before the September meeting, which is the window this trade lives in.

thesis: The market is pricing one hike and then a pause: 62c for a 25bp hike on Sep 16 but only 28c for another on Oct 28, with 69c on a hold. That structure assumes the energy shock is a one-off the Fed can look through. It is not one-off. Qatari LNG exports are down about 96% with the damaged trains estimated at three to five years of repair, Strait of Hormuz transit is largely halted after two tankers were struck on 2026-08-31, and the AAA national gasoline average printed $4.1203 on 2026-09-02 against $3.1869 a year ago — up 29% year over year and a record for the season. The September CPI release on Oct 13 is the first print that fully contains crude above $95, and it lands fifteen days before the October meeting. A committee that has already pushed the 10y to a 20-month high of 4.788% on hawkish signalling, and that has just restarted a hiking cycle, is more likely than 28% to go again with a hot print in hand. My estimate is about 40% against the market’s 28%, and the gap exists because the market is applying the standard central-bank playbook of looking through supply shocks to a shock whose supply loss is measured in years.
key_risk: This is a conditional bet stacked two deep: it needs the Fed to hike in September (62% priced) and then to hike again immediately (roughly 45% conditional). If the September meeting delivers a hike wrapped in explicit one-and-done language, this contract halves on the statement alone even though the thesis about inflation is intact. A US-Iran ceasefire collapses crude and takes the whole structure to single digits. The 15c stop is real but a 1c spread today can widen sharply once the September meeting resolves the interesting part of the distribution.
counter_argument: The strongest case against, and it is the textbook one: central banks are supposed to look through relative price shocks and target core, and core inflation is not what is moving here — energy is. An oil shock that takes gasoline up 29% year on year is a tax on consumption, so it is disinflationary for everything else with a lag, and hiking into it twice risks turning a supply shock into a recession. That is exactly why the market sits at 28c rather than 45c. The reason to take the other side is not that this reasoning is wrong but that this particular committee is visibly not following it — the 20-month-high 10y on hawkish signals is the evidence.

key_risk: Uranium equities trade as high-beta risk assets first and utility-linked contracts second — CCJ fell 2.53%, URA 3.45% and UEC 5.31% on 2026-09-01 during the very energy shock that is supposed to be their thesis. With a 4.29% ATR, this position can lose a fifth of its value in a market drawdown without a single fact about uranium changing. Invalidation, since a long-term hold carries no hard stop: the long-term uranium contract price falling back below $80/lb, or Kazatomprom restoring and then raising its output guidance — either means the supply tightness is over and the thesis is wrong at any price. A second invalidation is Westinghouse AP1000 orders failing to convert from the DOE commitment into signed reactor contracts over the next 18 months.
counter_argument: The strongest case against: this is the most crowded structural long in the market, it has been the consensus five-year story for three years running, and CCJ is still 28.8% below its high — which is evidence the thesis has been priced and re-priced rather than that it is undiscovered. Nuclear build cycles also slip by years as a matter of routine, so a 91-reactor pipeline and a conditional DOE commitment are not deliveries. Note too that the insider check returned zero transactions in either direction over six months, which for a Canadian issuer means the Form 4 data is simply uninformative here rather than a signal of any kind.

thesis: The cleanest way to be long expensive natural gas without owning a gas producer. US wholesale power prices are set at the margin by gas-fired generation, so when gas gets structurally dearer the operator whose fuel cost is not gas captures the whole difference — and Constellation runs the largest nuclear fleet in the country. The scarcity is now established rather than speculative: Qatari LNG exports are down about 96%, force majeure runs into November, and the damaged trains need three to five years. That divergence is the market beginning to price fuel position rather than the undifferentiated AI-datacenter-power theme, and CEG is the name on the right side of it.
key_risk: CEG is still a 16%-off-its-high member of a complex that is actively unwinding — Talen, NRG, Vistra and Argan are all down between 22% and 50% from their highs, and one session of relative strength is thin evidence that CEG has decoupled rather than merely lagged. If the AI-power theme is being de-rated wholesale, fuel economics will not save it. The 250 stop is 10.8% away, roughly 3.6 ATR, because a 3.02% daily ATR in a group behaving like this needs the room.
counter_argument: The strongest case against: nuclear generators are largely contracted forward through power purchase agreements, so the spot power price that gas is setting today reaches Constellation’s revenue with a multi-year lag, if at all — which makes the mechanism real but slow, and the stock is being priced on datacenter contracting news rather than on marginal fuel cost. It is also fair to say that the same LNG scarcity that lifts power prices raises the political risk of price caps and windfall interventions on inframarginal generators, which is precisely the profit this thesis is trying to capture.

thesis: The market is pricing one hike and then a pause — 62c for a 25bp hike on Sep 16 but only 28c for another on Oct 28, with 69c on a hold. That structure assumes the energy shock is a one-off the Fed can look through, and the supply loss says otherwise: Qatari LNG exports are down about 96% with the damaged trains estimated at three to five years of repair, Strait of Hormuz transit is largely halted after two tankers were struck on 2026-08-31, the US naval blockade remains in force with no US-Iran talks scheduled, and the AAA national gasoline average printed $4.1203 on 2026-09-02 against $3.1869 a year ago, up 29%. My estimate is about 35% against the market’s 28% — a real but modest edge, which is what a conviction-2 sizing is for.
key_risk: Thin evidence on the decisive variable, which is why this is a 2 and sized at 1%. The bet needs the Fed to hike twice in a row into a labour market that is already shrinking: payrolls fell 23,000 in July against a forecast of +80,000, after June was revised down to +20,000. A second negative print on Friday Sep 4 makes back-to-back hikes very hard to justify and this contract goes to the low teens. It is also conditional two deep — it needs the September hike (62%) and then an immediate repeat (roughly 45% conditional) — so a September hike delivered with explicit one-and-done language halves it on the statement alone, with the thesis about inflation entirely intact. A US-Iran ceasefire collapses crude and takes it to single digits.
counter_argument: The strongest case against is the textbook one and it has just gained evidence: central banks look through relative price shocks and target core, an oil shock that lifts gasoline 29% year on year is a tax on consumption and therefore disinflationary elsewhere with a lag, and hiking twice into a contracting labour market converts a supply shock into a recession. The July payroll print of -23,000 is exactly the data a committee would cite to stop after one. That is why the market sits at 28c, and it is a good reason — the position is a small bet that this specific committee, which has already pushed the 10y to a 20-month high on hawkish signalling, is not following the textbook.
